design_detail: Secondary analysis of personality data from an open-label, single-arm feasibility trial of psilocybin with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression at Imperial College London (trial reported by Carhart-Harris et al., 2016 and 2018, the paper's refs 22-23, not read here). 20 patients received oral psilocybin 10 mg and, one week later, 25 mg (study conditions), lying with eyes closed to a music playlist while two therapists took a non-directive, supportive role, with integration visits one day and one week after the 25 mg session. The NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (NEO PI-R) was completed at the screening visit and 3 months after; the 25 mg session was rated with the Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (ASC); depression with the QIDS-SR16. Paired t-tests with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction across the 5 domain and 30 facet scores; exploratory, uncorrected correlations with four ASC 'peak experience' factors and with depression change; responders compared with non-responders. No control group. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest (an uncontrolled before-after study of one treated group), appraised with ROBINS-I as for the other single-arm psychedelic-therapy studies in the card set (pp. 369-370).
can_establish: What happened to self-rated personality scores over 3 months in 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression who took part in an open-label psilocybin-with-support study (Neuroticism fell, Extraversion and Openness rose, Conscientiousness rose at trend level, Agreeableness did not change), and which changes went with depression improvement or with insightfulness during the session in exploratory, uncorrected correlations.
cannot_establish: That psilocybin caused these changes (no control group; the changes accompanied a fall in depression, which itself shifts how people describe their personality, and the authors concede the changes may be state rather than trait); that they last beyond 3 months; that the Openness rise is specific to psychedelic therapy (the comparison with antidepressant trials crosses studies, populations and follow-up times); or that behaviour changed (self-report only).

sample.recruitment: Patients with treatment-resistant depression enrolled in an open-label feasibility study; recruitment routes are described in the trial reports (refs 22-23), not here. A scripted telephone prescreen, then a screening visit at the Imperial Clinical Research Facility with physical and mental health history (MINI-5), blood tests, ECG, urine drug and pregnancy tests, breathalyser and baseline questionnaires including the NEO PI-R (Methods › Study procedure, 1st paragraph, p. 370).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: unipolar major depression of at least moderate severity (17 or more on the 21-item HAM-D) with no improvement despite two courses of pharmacologically distinct antidepressants of adequate duration (at least 6 weeks) in the current episode. Excluded: a current or previous psychotic disorder, or an immediate family member with one (Methods › Participants, pp. 369-370).
sample.demographics: Analysed 19: 6 women and 13 men, mean age 44.7 (SD 10.9, range 27-64) (p. 370). At baseline 18 of 20 had severe or very severe depression (QIDS-16 of 16 or more) and 2 moderate (11-15). Five had tried a psychedelic before, four of them recreationally in early adulthood; all but three had had psychological therapy or counselling (p. 370). Baseline NEO T scores (population mean 50, SD 10): Neuroticism 76.6, Extraversion 31.1, Openness 52.7, Agreeableness 46.8, Conscientiousness 29.9 (Table 1, p. 371).
sample.attrition: One of 20 patients chose not to complete most follow-up measures, including the 3-month NEO PI-R; 19 analysed (p. 370). How this patient differed at baseline is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Patients who volunteered for a trial of a psychedelic; the authors suggest that people low in Openness are less likely to volunteer for such a treatment, which may explain the above-average baseline Openness (Discussion, 10th paragraph, p. 374). Two-thirds were men (Limitations box, p. 368). Baseline Neuroticism, Extraversion and Conscientiousness were far from population norms, which leaves room for movement back towards them.

exposure.measurement: Assigned by the open-label protocol: psilocybin 10 mg, then 25 mg one week later. The acute experience of the 25 mg session was self-rated with the ASC; four factors linked to 'peak' experience were analysed: insightfulness, blissful state, experience of unity and spiritual experience (Methods › Measures and Analysis, p. 370).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral psilocybin 10 mg in the first session and 25 mg in the second, one week apart; a preparation visit before; patients lay with eyes closed listening to a music playlist with two therapists present; integration visits one day and one week after the 25 mg session (Methods › Study procedure, p. 370).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported in this paper; screening included a urine drug test and breathalyser (p. 370). Antidepressant or other treatment during the 3 months is not described here.

comparison.controls: None. Each patient's baseline score is the reference; changes are set against NEO PI-R norms (T = 50) and, in the Discussion, against effect sizes the authors computed from three antidepressant trials (five patient samples, 469 patients treated for 8-20 weeks) (Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs, p. 373).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality before the depressive episode is unknown; expectations of the treatment were not measured; concurrent treatment between the sessions and 3 months is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: NEO PI-R: five domains, each with six facets of eight items rated on a 5-point scale; raw scores converted to T scores with the combined-sex norms of the manual; at baseline and 3 months. ASC for the 25 mg session. QIDS-SR16 (and BDI) for depression (Methods › Measures, p. 370).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated, normed questionnaires. Self-rated Neuroticism and Extraversion are influenced by current mood; the authors concede it is hard to infer that the changes represent trait rather than state changes (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 373).
outcomes.operationalization: Personality change = paired difference in T score between baseline and 3 months. Treatment response = a fall of 50% or more in QIDS from baseline. Cohen's d computed from raw scores as the baseline mean minus the 3-month mean, divided by the square root of the sum of the two variances (Methods › Measures and Analysis, p. 370).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: False discovery rate (threshold 0.05) for the 35 paired t-tests of domains and facets; none for the correlation analyses, which the authors describe as uncorrected and exploratory (p. 370; Discussion, 12th paragraph, p. 375).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: self-report questionnaires in an open-label study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (T scores, baseline to 3 months; change; p; Cohen's d as printed): Neuroticism 76.6 to 70.9 (-5.7, p = 0.002, d -0.571); Extraversion 31.1 to 37.6 (+6.5, p < 0.001, d 0.716); Openness 52.7 to 57.6 (+4.9, p = 0.012, d 0.437); Agreeableness 46.8 to 46.7 (-0.1, p = 0.953, d -0.006); Conscientiousness 29.9 to 33.1 (+3.2, p = 0.086, d 0.273). Eleven of 30 facets changed at p < 0.05 and ten survived FDR correction (not Anxiety), among them Positive emotions +8.3 (d 0.740), Openness to Actions +7.5 (d 0.783), Vulnerability -7.3 (d -0.706) and Openness to Values +6.3 (d 0.692) (p. 371). Responders (n = 7) vs non-responders (n = 12): Neuroticism change -23 +/- 17 vs -6 +/- 8 (p = 0.038), Conscientiousness 15 +/- 11 vs 0 +/- 12 (p = 0.017), Openness 11 +/- 21 vs 7 +/- 6 (p = 0.623). Exploratory correlations (n = 19, uncorrected): insightfulness with Neuroticism change r = -0.47 (p = 0.043) and with Extraversion change r = 0.54 (p = 0.017); spiritual experience with Extraversion change r = 0.47 (p = 0.048); no peak-experience factor related to Openness or Conscientiousness change; no domain change correlated significantly with depression change (Neuroticism r = 0.41, p = 0.080; Extraversion r = -0.42, p = 0.071) (pp. 371-372). Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 19): 95% CI for r = -0.47 about -0.76 to -0.02, and for r = 0.54 about 0.11 to 0.80.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned in this paper; the trial reports (refs 22-23) were not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The SDs of the T scores are not reported, so the t-tests and effect sizes cannot be recomputed; the units of the responder comparison are not stated; a naturalistic survey cited in support of the Openness interpretation is unpublished, with data not shown (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 373).
analysis.power: No power calculation; the authors note that the modest sample limits power, particularly for the responder subgroups (Discussion, 12th paragraph, p. 375).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression, self-rated Neuroticism fell (T 76.6 to 70.9) and Extraversion (31.1 to 37.6) and Openness (52.7 to 57.6) rose between baseline and 3 months after open-label psilocybin with psychological support; Conscientiousness rose at trend level (p = 0.086) and Agreeableness did not change. Neuroticism and Conscientiousness changed more in the 7 responders than in the 12 non-responders; the Openness rise did not differ by response and did not correlate with depression change. In uncorrected correlations, insightfulness during the 25 mg session went with larger Neuroticism falls and Extraversion rises; no peak-experience factor went with the Openness rise.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the Neuroticism and Extraversion changes were 'predicted' by insightfulness, which rests on two uncorrected correlations in 19 people (r = -0.47, p = 0.043; r = 0.54, p = 0.017). The conclusion that the pronounced increases in Extraversion and Openness 'might constitute an effect more specific to psychedelic therapy' (p. 368) rests on comparing this uncontrolled study's d values with values computed from antidepressant trials in other populations, with follow-up of 8-20 weeks; the paper itself says such comparisons should be made cautiously (p. 373), and the printed d formula gives smaller values than the usual average-SD d (see reporting issues). The Discussion's statement that a single profound psychedelic experience 'can lead to lasting changes in personality' (p. 374) uses a causal verb and 'lasting' for an uncontrolled 3-month observation, while the authors elsewhere concede it is hard to infer that the Neuroticism and Extraversion changes are trait rather than state changes (p. 373). Support from an unpublished naturalistic survey is cited with data not shown (p. 373). The Limitations box and the Discussion acknowledge the small sample, open-label design, absence of a control condition and exploratory correlations (pp. 368, 375).

timeline.event: MacLean et al.: in healthy hallucinogen-naive volunteers, self-rated Openness rose 1-2 months after high-dose psilocybin, concentrated in those with a complete mystical experience.
Carhart-Harris et al. (2016): small increases in Openness in healthy volunteers 2 weeks after LSD, as described in this paper (p. 374).
Wagner et al. (2017): MDMA with psychotherapy for PTSD followed by increased Openness and decreased Neuroticism, as described in this paper (p. 374).
Schmid & Liechti (2018): an LSD study with 1- and 12-month follow-ups did not replicate an Openness increase, as described in this paper (p. 374).

Timmermann et al. analyse metaphysical-belief data from the same group's randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021), a direct comparison of the kind the authors said they were setting up (p. 373); personality outcomes from that trial were not among the sources read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Self-rated Openness rose after psilocybin both in the healthy-volunteer analysis by MacLean et al. (2011) and in this uncontrolled patient study, but the two disagree on the role of the acute experience (mystical experience there; insightfulness, and not for Openness, here), which the authors discuss (p. 375); neither had a randomized comparison of personality change. In depression, falls in Neuroticism and rises in Extraversion are expected with any successful treatment, as the authors note from antidepressant trials (p. 372). Whether psychedelic therapy changes personality more than other effective treatments needs a controlled trial with personality as a pre-specified outcome.

funding.funder: No funding section. The Acknowledgements state that the research was carried out at the NIHR/Wellcome Trust Imperial Clinical Research Facility and thank the Medical Research Council (MRC), the Beckley Foundation, Compass Pathways and the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust (p. 376).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre for Neuropsychopharmacology, Imperial College London, the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and King's College London; K. MacLean, first author of MacLean et al. (2011), is listed in Sherman, CT, USA. Four organisations are thanked in the Acknowledgements while the Declaration of interests reads 'None'; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in depression comparing psilocybin therapy with an equally intensive active treatment, with personality (self-rated and rated by someone who knows the patient) as a pre-specified outcome at baseline, at the end of treatment and at 12 months, analysed with depression change as a covariate to separate trait from state effects, and with expectations measured before treatment.

domains.note: No comparison group. The 3-month change mixes any effect of psilocybin with the fall in depression (which shifts self-rated Neuroticism and Extraversion), the psychological support and integration visits, expectations, regression from extreme baseline scores (Neuroticism T 76.6, Extraversion 31.1, Conscientiousness 29.9) and the passage of time.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers for a psychedelic trial with above-average baseline Openness; selection bears more on who the results apply to than on the change itself.
Everyone followed the same protocol (10 mg, then 25 mg).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Antidepressants, therapy or other treatment between the sessions and 3 months are not reported in this paper.
19 of 20 analysed; one patient declined most follow-up measures.
Self-rated questionnaires completed by patients who knew they had received psilocybin in a study expected to help them; no informant ratings.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: FDR correction across all 35 scores is a strength, but uncorrected exploratory correlations are presented in the abstract as 'predicted' changes; no registration mentioned; SDs not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that psilocybin changes personality, the study is at critical risk of bias: there is no comparison group, the outcomes are self-rated by unblinded patients whose depression was improving, and extreme baseline scores are open to regression toward the norm. The card may be cited for what was observed in these 19 patients (Neuroticism down 5.7 T points, Extraversion up 6.5 and Openness up 4.9 at 3 months; Agreeableness unchanged), for the finding that the Openness rise did not track depression improvement, and for the authors' own caveat that the changes may reflect state rather than trait; not for a causal or psychedelic-specific effect, or for permanence.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: 20 patients with treatment-resistant depression (HAM-D of 17 or more; no improvement after two distinct antidepressant courses) received open-label oral psilocybin 10 mg and, one week later, 25 mg with psychological support (study conditions); personality (NEO PI-R) at baseline and 3 months; 19 analysed (6 women, 13 men, mean age 44.7, SD 10.9); 18 of 20 had severe or very severe depression at baseline; five had used a psychedelic before.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants; Study procedure; Results, 1st paragraph (p. 370)

key_findings.finding: From baseline to 3 months, three of five domains changed significantly: Neuroticism T 76.6 to 70.9 (-5.7, p = 0.002, d -0.571), Extraversion 31.1 to 37.6 (+6.5, p < 0.001, d 0.716) and Openness 52.7 to 57.6 (+4.9, p = 0.012, d 0.437); Conscientiousness rose 3.2 at trend level (29.9 to 33.1, p = 0.086); Agreeableness did not change (46.8 to 46.7, p = 0.953).
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality changes from baseline to 3-month follow-up, 1st paragraph (p. 370, continuing on p. 371); Table 1 (p. 371)
key_findings.note: The printed d values use a formula with a larger denominator than the usual average-SD d (see reporting issues); SDs are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Eleven of 30 facets changed at p < 0.05, all within Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness and Conscientiousness, and ten survived FDR correction (Anxiety did not): for example Positive emotions +8.3, Openness to Actions +7.5, Vulnerability -7.3, Warmth +7.1, Depression -6.6, Openness to Values +6.3, Competence +6.3 T points.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnote; Results › Personality changes from baseline to 3-month follow-up, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Responders at 3 months (n = 7) showed larger falls in Neuroticism than non-responders (n = 12) (-23 +/- 17 vs -6 +/- 8, p = 0.038) and larger rises in Conscientiousness (15 +/- 11 vs 0 +/- 12, p = 0.017), but did not differ in Openness (11 +/- 21 vs 7 +/- 6, p = 0.623), Agreeableness (p = 0.577) or Extraversion (p = 0.105).
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality changes vs. changes in depression scores, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The units of these values are not stated; their size relative to the T-score changes suggests raw scores (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: No domain change correlated significantly with the change in QIDS or BDI depression scores at 3 months; the Neuroticism decrease (r = 0.41, p = 0.080) and Extraversion increase (r = -0.42, p = 0.071) went with QIDS decreases at trend level only.
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality changes vs. changes in depression scores, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In exploratory, uncorrected correlations (n = 19), insightfulness during the 25 mg session went with a larger fall in Neuroticism (r = -0.47, p = 0.043) and a larger rise in Extraversion (r = 0.54, p = 0.017); spiritual experience went with the Extraversion rise (r = 0.47, p = 0.048); blissful state (r = 0.41, p = 0.081) and experience of unity (r = 0.42, p = 0.075) only at trend level; no peak-experience score related to the change in Openness or Conscientiousness.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship between Peak Experience and personality changes, 1st paragraph (p. 371, continuing on p. 372)
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% CIs (Fisher z): r = -0.47, about -0.76 to -0.02; r = 0.54, about 0.11 to 0.80.

key_findings.finding: Baseline personality and the acute experience: baseline Openness went with blissful state only at trend level (r = 0.43, p = 0.063); among its facets, Openness to Fantasy correlated with blissful state (r = 0.50, p = 0.030). Higher baseline Neuroticism went with less improvement in depression at trend level (r = -0.42, p = 0.075); responders did not differ from non-responders on any baseline domain.
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline personality scores as predictors of Peak Experience, 1st paragraph; Baseline personality scores as predictors of treatment response, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline Openness was already 2.7 T points above the norm and rose a further 4.9 points, whereas Neuroticism fell from an abnormally high level and Extraversion and Conscientiousness rose from abnormally low levels, that is, towards the scores of healthy people; the authors suggest that people low in Openness are less likely to volunteer for a psychedelic treatment.

Comparison with antidepressant trials computed by the authors (five patient samples from three trials, 469 patients treated for 8-20 weeks): sample-size-weighted d for Neuroticism, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness -0.59, 0.04 and 0.18 there vs -0.57, -0.01 and 0.27 here; for Openness 0.13 vs 0.44 and for Extraversion 0.32 vs 0.72. The authors caution that differing follow-up times call for caution in comparing d values across studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (continuing in the right column) and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that from these data it is hard to infer that the NEO PI-R changes, particularly in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are trait rather than state changes, though a change lasting 3 months might suggest it is not only a state artefact.

The authors call their findings somewhat inconsistent with MacLean et al. (2011), where mystical-type experience predicted sustained Openness increases, and suggest differences in population, in questionnaires for the acute experience, in the support offered (for example emphasis on mystical experience during preparation) and in timing (3 months here vs more than 12 there).

reporting_issues.issue: Cohen's d is defined as the difference in means divided by the square root of the sum of the two variances, without dividing that sum by 2; applied as printed, this gives values about 0.71 times (1/square root of 2) the usual average-SD d (editors' calculation). The SDs are not reported, so the values cannot be checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed d values (for example 0.437 for Openness) may understate the standardized changes by about 30%; if the same formula was used for the antidepressant comparison, the ratios between studies are unaffected, but the absolute sizes cannot be compared with d values from other sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 labels Openness to Values with P = 0.002, while Table 1 gives 0.001; it labels Positive emotions 'P > 0.001', while Table 1 gives 0.000 (that is, below 0.001).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both facets are significant in either version.

reporting_issues.issue: The responder comparison reports changes such as -23 +/- 17 without stating the unit; T-score changes for the whole group are 3-7 points, so these are presumably raw scores.
reporting_issues.consequence: The values cannot be compared directly with Table 1 and should not be quoted as T-score changes.

reporting_issues.issue: The spiritual-experience correlation is printed as r = 0.47 with p = 0.048, while the insightfulness correlation of the same size (r = -0.47) has p = 0.043, the value expected with n = 19 (editors' calculation); the number of patients behind each correlation is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one of the correlations may rest on 18 patients or carry a rounding difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Support for the Openness interpretation is drawn from the authors' unpublished naturalistic survey of more than 200 people ('manuscript in prep, data not shown').
reporting_issues.consequence: That support cannot be checked from the paper.
